FortiBleed 'adminin' backdoor local account creation and logon AIInstallation High
Hunts creation and subsequent use of a local account named 'adminin' — the exact backdoor username SOCRadar found planted on FortiBleed-compromised systems for persistent access. Fires on both the account-creation command and any logon by that account. Rationale: Anchored on the exact backdoor username 'adminin' from the article's code block; SOCRadar/SecurityWeek independently confirm the operators 'make backdoor users' on compromised FortiBleed hosts, making this a near-zero-FP named-account detection. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-fortinet-firewalls-compromised/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/active-fortibleed-campaign-impacting-fortinet-devices-across-194-countries/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1078.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An organization legitimately standardizes admin service accounts on a similar naming scheme (e.g. 'adminintl' truncated in a script)
  • Red-team / purple-team exercise recreating the FortiBleed backdoor for detection validation
  • IT provisioning template that reuses a generic bootstrap account name
  • Migration tooling that recreates local accounts during OS re-imaging
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DeviceProcessEvents/4720 record — who (InitiatingProcessAccountName) created 'adminin', from what parent process, and whether it was added to Administrators/Remote Desktop groups. Correlate the logon RemoteIP against known-good admin subnets. 2) Contain: disable/delete the 'adminin' account, force-reset any admin credentials on the host, and isolate the device from the network if it is an internet-facing appliance mgmt host. 3) Hunt: sweep every host and FortiGate for the same account name, look for outbound connections to unfamiliar hosting IPs, and check for downloaded FortiGate config files and the FortigateSniffer tool.
union
 (DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "adminin"
  | where (FileName in~ ("net.exe","net1.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "user" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/add","-add"))
       or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("New-LocalUser","Add-LocalGroupMember"))
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="LocalAccountCreated", Account="adminin", Detail=ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
 (DeviceLogonEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where AccountName =~ "adminin"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="BackdoorAccountLogon", Account=AccountName, Detail=strcat("LogonType=", tostring(LogonType), " RemoteIP=", RemoteIP), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountDomain)
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (EventID in (4720,4732,4728,4726) and TargetUserName =~ "adminin")
     or (EventID == 4624 and TargetUserName =~ "adminin")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, Activity, TargetUserName, SubjectUserName, IpAddress, LogonType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/\bnet1?\s+user\s+adminin\b.*(\/add|-add)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine], function=count(as=execCount))

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("net.exe","net1.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")) Processes.process="*adminin*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process,"(?i)(user\s+adminin.*(/add|-add)|New-LocalUser.*adminin|Add-LocalGroupMember.*adminin)") | sort - lastTime
Credential-stuffing burst culminating in success against FortiGate SSL-VPN / SSO AIExploitation Medium
Detects the FortiBleed reuse pattern: many failed authentications from a single source IP across multiple usernames followed by at least one success — the harvested/cracked Fortinet credentials being stuffed against SSL-VPN gateways and reused against Entra SSO. Rationale: The article and multiple corroborating sources state credential stuffing is the PRIMARY collection/reuse mechanism of FortiBleed; the one-IP/many-users/many-fails-then-success shape against FortiGate SSL-VPN and Entra SSO is the article-specific signature of stolen-credential reuse, not a generic brute-force template. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/what-is-fortibleed/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortibleed-86000-fortinet-device-credentials-compromised/ • https://www.bitsight.com/blog/security-alert-fortibleed-fortinet-vpn-credentials-firewall-exposed
ATT&CKT1110.004 T1110.003 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate NAT/VPN concentrator egressing many users behind one public IP triggering the distinct-user threshold
  • Misconfigured mobile client or expired-password loop generating repeated failures then a success after reset
  • Security scanner / authenticated vulnerability scan hitting the VPN portal
  • SSO migration event causing bulk re-authentication from a proxy IP
Suppression filter
// exclude known corporate egress / NAT gateways before alerting:
| where SourceIP !in ("") // populate with your published corporate egress IPs; keep external-only IPs in scope
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not a corporate NAT gateway; enumerate which usernames succeeded and whether MFA was satisfied. 2) Contain: force password reset + session revocation on every successfully-authenticated account from that IP, block the source IP at the FortiGate and IdP, and enforce MFA on SSL-VPN if absent. 3) Hunt: check whether any of the compromised accounts have Fortinet-managed credentials matching the FortiBleed dumps, review those accounts for 'adminin' creation, config downloads, and lateral movement toward file servers/backup hosts.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| summarize Failures = countif(ErrorCode != 0), Successes = countif(ErrorCode == 0), DistinctUsers = dcount(AccountUpn), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), SampleApps = make_set(Application, 5) by IPAddress
| where DistinctUsers >= 10 and Failures >= 20 and Successes >= 1   // one IP, 10+ users, 20+ fails, >=1 success = stuffing signature
| order by Failures desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Activity has_any ("ssl-login","sslvpn","vpn","login") or Message has_any ("SSL VPN","login")
| extend Outcome = tolower(coalesce(EventOutcome, DeviceAction, Message))
| summarize Failures = countif(Outcome has_any ("fail","deny","error")), Successes = countif(Outcome has_any ("success","accept","ok","tunnel-up")), DistinctUsers = dcount(DestinationHostName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SourceIP
| where DistinctUsers >= 10 and Failures >= 20 and Successes >= 1
| order by Failures desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:50126
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where (Authentication.app="fortigate" OR Authentication.app="*ssl*vpn*" OR Authentication.app="*vpn*") by Authentication.src Authentication.action Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes dc(user) as user_count values(user) as users by src | where failures >= 20 AND successes >= 1 AND user_count >= 10 | sort - failures
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where (Authentication.app="fortigate" OR Authentication.app="*ssl*vpn*" OR Authentication.app="*vpn*") by Authentication.src Authentication.action Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | stats sum(eval(if(action="failure",count,0))) as failures sum(eval(if(action="success",count,0))) as successes dc(user) as user_count values(user) as users by src | where failures >= 20 AND successes >= 1 AND user_count >= 10 | sort - failures
FortiGate admin login and configuration download from external IP AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the FortiBleed initial-access footprint on edge devices: administrative authentication to a FortiGate from a public/Internet source IP paired with configuration backup/download activity — the exact behaviour that produced the exposed cache of FortiGate config files. Rationale: Anchored on the article's 'downloaded FortiGate configuration files' collection artifact plus the mass edge-device compromise; scoping FortiGate config-download/admin-login to a non-private (external) source IP flags attacker administrative access rather than internal management. Defender/Falcon/Datadog left empty as FortiGate appliance logs do not ship to those platforms. Cross-checked against: • https://socradar.io/blog/fortibleed-fortinet-firewalls-compromised/ • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4186790/fortibleed-campaign-exposes-75000-fortinet-firewalls-worldwide.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1602.002 T1078
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote administrator managing the FortiGate over the public interface from a home/ISP IP
  • MSP/outsourced NOC performing scheduled configuration backups from their own cloud IP
  • Vendor support session downloading config for troubleshooting
  • Monitoring tool pulling config snapshots via API from an external SaaS source
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in ("") // populate with approved external management source IPs (MSP/NOC/admin home IPs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the admin account and source IP; verify against the approved management-IP allowlist and change-management tickets for a config backup at that time. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, disable/rotate the admin credential, restrict the mgmt interface to trusted IPs / VPN only, and pull the current config to diff against baseline for rogue admins ('adminin'), added VPN users, or a packet-sniffer/FortigateSniffer artifact. 3) Hunt: review VPN auth logs for stuffing bursts, check for outbound connections to unfamiliar hosting IPs, and correlate the org against INC/Lynx leak-site listings.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where Message has_any ("Configuration is downloaded","config backup","backup config","Admin login successful","login successful") or Activity has_any ("download","backup","admin-login")
| extend SrcIP = SourceIP
| where isnotempty(SrcIP) and not(ipv4_is_private(SrcIP))
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName = DeviceExternalID, SrcIP, DestinationHostName, SourceUserName, Activity, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate" Authentication.action="success" (Authentication.user="admin" OR Authentication.user="*admin*") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.app="fortigate" Authentication.action="success" (Authentication.user="admin" OR Authentication.user="*admin*") by Authentication.src Authentication.dest Authentication.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | where NOT (cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8",src) OR cidrmatch("172.16.0.0/12",src) OR cidrmatch("192.168.0.0/16",src)) | sort - lastTime
Outbound connection to FortiBleed operator infrastructure 85.11.187.8 AICommand & Control Low
Watches for any host or edge device communicating with 85.11.187.8, the FortiBleed operator server IP surfaced in the article. Single-source IOC — ship as hunting/enrichment, validate before alerting. Rationale: Uses the single pre-extracted network IOC (85.11.187.8) from the article. It could NOT be corroborated by a second source (ThreatFox/OTX/other vendor write-ups), so confidence is Low and it is scoped as hunting/enrichment — validate reputation before alerting.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The IP is shared hosting and later serves a benign tenant after takedown/reassignment
  • Threat-intel or ASM scanner in your environment probing the flagged IP
  • Security researcher/sandbox traffic to the IP from a lab host
  • Stale IOC firing on historical benign traffic if the address was previously legitimate
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm current reputation of 85.11.187.8 (VT/ThreatFox/passive DNS) and identify the initiating process/user and data volume (bytes out). 2) Contain: block the IP at perimeter/EDR, and if the source is a FortiGate or server staging harvested data, isolate it. 3) Hunt: expand to the wider operator fleet by pivoting on ASN/hosting neighbors, look for config/credential archive uploads, 'adminin' accounts, and any Lynx/INC follow-on activity on the same host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.11.187.8"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
 (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationIP == "85.11.187.8" or SourceIP == "85.11.187.8" | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, SentBytes, ReceivedBytes, SourceUserName),
 (ImNetworkSession | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DstIpAddr == "85.11.187.8" or SrcIpAddr == "85.11.187.8" | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects network connections to 85.11.187.8, an IP tied to FortiBleed operator infrastructure in the source article. Single-source IOC — validate before promoting to alerting.

#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=85.11.187.8
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemotePort], function=count(as=connCount))
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes_out from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.dest="85.11.187.8" OR All_Traffic.src="85.11.187.8") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | sort - lastTime

Lynx/INC ransomware mass file encryption via .lynx extension AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the impact stage the FortiBleed access ultimately fed: bulk creation/rename of files with the '.lynx' extension by a single process, the hallmark of Lynx (INC rebrand) ransomware encryption. Corroborated extension across multiple vendor analyses. Rationale: The article explicitly links FortiBleed access to Lynx/INC ransomware impact; Unit42, Nextron, FortiGuard and Rapid7 independently confirm Lynx appends the unique '.lynx' extension and drops README.txt, so bulk '.lynx' writes by one process is a high-fidelity, article-specific impact detection. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/inc-ransomware-rebrand-to-lynx/ • https://www.nextron-systems.com/2024/10/11/in-depth-analysis-of-lynx-ransomware/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/ransomware-roundup-lynx • https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/2024/09/12/ransomware-groups-demystified-lynx-ransomware/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate application or dataset that coincidentally uses a '.lynx' file extension (rare; e.g. niche lynx browser cache/config artifacts)
  • Backup/restore of a previously-encrypted dataset re-introducing .lynx files
  • Security team detonating a Lynx sample in a sandbox on a monitored host
  • Renaming utility batch-appending '.lynx' during a controlled DFIR exercise
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and account, confirm whether README.txt ransom notes were dropped in the same directories and whether Volume Shadow Copies were deleted. 2) Contain: immediately isolate the host from the network, kill/suspend the encrypting process, and preserve memory and a disk image; check for spread to file servers/backup infrastructure (Veeam/MSSQL/Exchange). 3) Hunt: trace the intrusion back — FortiGate VPN stuffing logins, 'adminin' backdoor accounts, config downloads, and outbound staging to unfamiliar hosting IPs — and cross-reference the org against INC/Lynx leak-site listings; engage IR and preserve keys for possible decryption recovery.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName endswith ".lynx"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(FolderPath), SampleFiles = make_set(FileName, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Proc = any(InitiatingProcessFileName), ProcCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where FileCount >= 25   // 25 = mass-encryption burst; lower to 1 for max sensitivity given unique extension
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "lynx" or TargetFileName endswith ".lynx"
| summarize FileCount = dcount(TargetFilePath), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Proc = any(ActingProcessName) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileCount >= 25
| order by FirstSeen desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-24858")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-24858")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New ChocoPoC malware targets researchers via trojanized PoC exploits

BleepingComputer
2026-07-01 7 use cases 3 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Multiple weaponized proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits on GitHub were found delivering a Python-based remote access trojan (RAT) named ChocoPoC that can execute commands and steal sensitive data in a campaign believed to target cybersecurity researchers. [...]

CVEsCVE-2025-64446 CVE-2025-55182 CVE-2025-14847 CVE-2026-0257 CVE-2026-10520 CVE-2026-50751 CVE-2026-48908
ATT&CKT1190 T1204.002 T1555.003
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance
Detected
Phase 2
Weaponization
Detected
Phase 3
Delivery
Detected
Phase 4
Exploitation
Detected
Phase 5
Installation
Detected
Phase 6
Command & Control
Detected
Phase 7
Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] ChocoPoC supply-chain: malicious PyPI packages (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt) installed via cloned PoC repo
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] ChocoPoC native Python extension (skytext .so/.pyd) loaded by interpreter for embedded-code decryption
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] ChocoPoC C2/exfil: Python process contacting Mapbox dataset API
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] ChocoPoC credential access: non-browser process reading multiple browser secret stores · [LLM] ChocoPoC discovery: bulk enumeration of docs/DB files and shell history by a Python process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
ChocoPoC supply-chain: malicious PyPI packages (frint/skytext/slogsec/logcrypt) installed via cloned PoC repo AIDelivery High
Hunts installation of the specific trojanized PyPI packages that carry the ChocoPoC infection chain, dropped under site-packages when a victim clones one of the weaponized GitHub PoC repos and runs pip. Article-specific because it keys on the four named packages, not on generic pip activity. Rationale: Anchors on the four literal package names Sekoia named (frint, skytext, slogsec, logcrypt.cryptography) landing in site-packages via a pip/python installer — high fidelity because no legitimate package shares these obfuscated names. Cross-checked against the second BleepingComputer/Sekoia write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/ • https://www.sekoia.com/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A researcher legitimately investigating the campaign detonates the package in a monitored sandbox
  • An internal package genuinely named with a colliding substring (e.g. 'logcrypto', 'skytextures') is installed
  • Security team mirrors the malicious package into an internal artifact repo for analysis
  • Automated dependency-scanning tooling downloads the package to inspect it
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("--dry-run","pip download","--no-deps") or DeviceName has_any ("malware-sandbox","detonation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine and the parent directory of the pip invocation — confirm it originated from a freshly git-cloned CVE-*-PoC repo and identify the requirements/setup that pulled the dep. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill python/pip processes, remove the site-packages/{frint,skytext,slogsec,logcrypt} dirs, and rotate any credentials the user could reach (browser, SSH, cloud). 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound mapbox.com traffic and browser-secret-store access (UC3/UC4) and sweep other researcher endpoints that cloned the same repo.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "site-packages"
| where FolderPath has_any ("frint","skytext","slogsec","logcrypt")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3","uv") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip","pip3 install")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "site-packages"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("frint","skytext","slogsec","logcrypt")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("pip","pip3","python","python3","uv") or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChocoPoC Trojanized PyPI Package Dropped Under site-packages
id: 5b6f2a10-4c3d-4e21-9a77-1f0c9b8e2a41
description: Detects file writes of the ChocoPoC campaign's malicious PyPI packages (frint, skytext, slogsec, logcrypt) into a Python site-packages directory by a pip/python installer.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.t1204.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains: 'site-packages'
  selection_pkg:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - 'frint'
      - 'skytext'
      - 'slogsec'
      - 'logcrypt'
  condition: selection_path and selection_pkg
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.command_line:(*frint* OR *skytext* OR *slogsec* OR *logcrypt*) @process.name:(pip OR pip3 OR python OR python3 OR uv)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten | TargetFileName=/site-packages.*(frint|skytext|slogsec|logcrypt)/i | ContextImageFileName=/(pip|python|uv)/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*frint*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*skytext*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*slogsec*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*logcrypt*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
ChocoPoC native Python extension (skytext .so/.pyd) loaded by interpreter for embedded-code decryption AIInstallation High
Detects the second-stage step where the compiled native extension shipped in the malicious 'skytext' package is loaded/executed by the Python interpreter, which then decrypts embedded Python and stages the downloader. Keys on the skytext package path plus a native module (.so/.pyd), not generic module loading. Rationale: Ties the article's 'skytext contains a compiled native Python extension … runs automatically and decrypts embedded Python code' to a concrete telemetry event: a .so/.pyd inside the skytext site-packages dir being loaded by python. Datadog left empty — standard Datadog Sysmon fields don't include image-load (EID7) and Linux .so loads aren't shipped via auditd. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-exploits-on-github/
ATT&CKT1027 T1140 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst re-runs the sample in a sandbox and the extension loads legitimately during analysis
  • A benign package unrelated to the campaign happens to vendor a native module under a directory containing the 'frint' substring
  • Reverse-engineering of the collected sample on an EDR-monitored workstation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the loading python process's working directory maps to a cloned PoC repo and capture the SHA256 of the .so/.pyd for reputation lookup. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the python process tree, quarantine the skytext package directory, and snapshot memory if in-scope (embedded code is decrypted in-process). 3) Hunt: immediately check the same host and time window for the downloader reaching a Mapbox dataset (UC3) and for browser-credential access (UC4).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "site-packages"
| where FolderPath has_any ("skytext","frint")
| where FileName endswith ".so" or FileName endswith ".pyd"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "site-packages"
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("skytext","frint")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".so" or TargetFileName endswith ".pyd"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ChocoPoC Native Python Extension Loaded From skytext Package
id: 9d1c7e44-2b8a-4f30-b6c1-7a2e5d9f3b02
description: Detects the Python interpreter loading a native extension (.so/.pyd) from the malicious skytext/frint site-packages directory, the ChocoPoC decryption/staging step.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1027
  - attack.t1140
  - attack.t1059.006
logsource:
  category: image_load
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|contains: 'site-packages'
    ImageLoaded|contains:
      - 'skytext'
      - 'frint'
  ext:
    ImageLoaded|endswith:
      - '.so'
      - '.pyd'
  condition: selection and ext
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo | TargetFileName=/site-packages.*(skytext|frint).*\.(so|pyd)$/i | ContextImageFileName=/python/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*skytext*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*frint*") (Filesystem.file_name="*.so" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.pyd") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*skytext*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*site-packages*frint*") (Filesystem.file_name="*.so" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.pyd") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
ChocoPoC C2/exfil: Python process contacting Mapbox dataset API AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the ChocoPoC command-and-control and exfiltration channel — a Python (or curl/wget) process reaching mapbox.com / api.mapbox.com to pull the final payload and stage stolen data via Mapbox datasets. Scoped to script-interpreter initiators so it isn't just normal browser/GIS map traffic. Rationale: Mapbox is a legitimate service, so this pivots on the article's specific abuse — a non-browser script interpreter (python/curl/wget) talking to mapbox.com/datasets for payload retrieval and exfil. DNS-from-python (Falcon) is the cleanest cross-platform pivot; Sentinel uses ImWebSession as DeviceNetworkEvents has no process-attributed equivalent there. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/ • https://www.sekoia.com/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1071.001 T1567.002
Data sourcesWeb Network_Resolution
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data scientists using python plotly/folium/geopandas or the official mapbox SDK to render maps
  • GIS/mapping automation pipelines calling api.mapbox.com from python
  • curl/wget scripts pulling Mapbox tiles or datasets for legitimate app dev
  • CI jobs that fetch Mapbox styles/tokens during build
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("folium","plotly","geopandas","mapboxgl","contextily"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full URL path and HTTP method — dataset GETs pulling an executable payload or PUT/POST of large encoded bodies to /datasets/ is the tell versus tile rendering; correlate the process to a recent skytext install (UC1/UC2). 2) Contain: isolate host, block the specific Mapbox dataset/account resource at proxy, kill the python process, and revoke any Mapbox tokens the host used. 3) Hunt: search the same process for browser-secret access and sensitive-file enumeration (UC4/UC5), and pull any parallel HTTP-server upload channel the article notes is used for larger files.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "mapbox.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","curl","wget")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize Conns = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Urls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "mapbox.com" or HttpHostName has "mapbox"
| where Url has "/datasets/" or HttpMethod in ("PUT","POST","PATCH") or Url has "mapbox.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Url, HttpMethod, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpResponseBodyBytes, HttpRequestBodyBytes
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Python Process DNS Lookup for Mapbox (ChocoPoC C2/Exfil)
id: 2f8b41c9-6d3e-4a15-8f70-c4b9a0d21e53
description: Detects a Python interpreter resolving mapbox.com, matching the ChocoPoC downloader/exfil channel that abuses Mapbox datasets.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1102.002
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.t1567.002
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|contains: 'mapbox.com'
    Image|contains:
      - 'python'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR */python OR */python3) @DestinationHostname:(*mapbox.com* OR *Mapbox.com*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest | DomainName=/mapbox\.com/i | ContextImageFileName=/(python|curl|wget)/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Web.url) as urls from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*mapbox.com*" AND (Web.app="python" OR Web.app="python3" OR Web.app="curl" OR Web.app="wget") by Web.src Web.dest Web.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.url) as urls from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*mapbox.com*" AND (Web.app="python" OR Web.app="python3" OR Web.app="curl" OR Web.app="wget") by Web.src Web.dest Web.app | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
ChocoPoC credential access: non-browser process reading multiple browser secret stores AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the ChocoPoC RAT harvesting browser passwords, cookies, autofill and history — a python/shell process touching two or more browser credential stores (Login Data, Cookies, key4.db, logins.json, etc.) in a burst while excluding the browsers themselves. Article-specific to the stealer capability list. Rationale: Maps the article's exact stealer capability (browser passwords, cookies, autofill, history) to a non-browser interpreter touching >=2 named secret stores in a burst — the dcount>=2 threshold and browser-process exclusion keep TP fidelity high. Datadog left empty as credential-store reads aren't captured by standard auditd EXECVE or Sysmon file-create telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate password-manager importer (KeePassXC/Bitwarden CLI) reading browser stores for migration
  • Backup tooling (rclone/restic/borg) snapshotting a user profile directory
  • IT profile-migration scripts copying browser data between machines
  • Browser-sync/decrypt research tooling run by the security team itself
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !has_any ("keepassxc","bitwarden","rclone","restic","borg","duplicati")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reading process is not a sanctioned migration/backup tool and correlate to a recent skytext install or PoC clone on the same host and user. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the process, and force-reset the user's browser-saved passwords and invalidate active web sessions/cookies (cookie theft = session hijack risk). 3) Hunt: check for outbound Mapbox exfil (UC3) carrying the harvested data and enumerate other researcher endpoints touching the same stores in the window.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("google-chrome","chromium","BraveSoftware","Microsoft Edge","microsoft-edge",".mozilla","Firefox")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","Local State","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite","formhistory.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash","curl")
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("chrome","msedge","firefox","brave","chromium","opera"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize StoresTouched = dcount(FileName), Stores = make_set(FileName, 20), Profiles = make_set(FolderPath, 10), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where StoresTouched >= 2
| order by bin_Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("google-chrome","chromium","BraveSoftware","Microsoft Edge","microsoft-edge",".mozilla","Firefox")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","Web Data","Local State","logins.json","key4.db","cookies.sqlite","places.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3","sh","bash","dash","curl")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome","msedge","firefox","brave","chromium","opera"))
| summarize StoresTouched = dcount(TargetFileName), Stores = make_set(TargetFileName, 20), SampleCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where StoresTouched >= 2
| order by bin_TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-Browser Process Reads Browser Credential Store (ChocoPoC Stealer)
id: 7c0a93de-5f21-4b88-9d34-2ea6f1c7b490
description: Detects a script interpreter (python/shell/curl) accessing a browser credential or cookie store, matching the ChocoPoC browser-credential harvesting capability.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/new-chocopoc-malware-targets-researchers-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1539
  - attack.t1005
logsource:
  category: file_access
detection:
  selection_file:
    FileName:
      - 'Login Data'
      - 'Cookies'
      - 'Web Data'
      - 'key4.db'
      - 'logins.json'
      - 'cookies.sqlite'
  selection_proc:
    Image|contains:
      - 'python'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - 'curl'
  filter_browser:
    Image|contains:
      - 'chrome'
      - 'firefox'
      - 'msedge'
      - 'brave'
  condition: selection_file and selection_proc and not filter_browser
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo | TargetFileName=/(Login Data|Cookies|Web Data|Local State|logins\.json|key4\.db|cookies\.sqlite)/i | ContextImageFileName=/(python|bash|/sh|dash|curl)/i | NOT ContextImageFileName=/(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|chromium|opera)/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true)) | _count >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Filesystem.file_name) as stores values(Filesystem.file_name) as files min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*google-chrome*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*chromium*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*BraveSoftware*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.mozilla*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Microsoft*Edge*") (Filesystem.file_name="Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Cookies" OR Filesystem.file_name="Web Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="key4.db" OR Filesystem.file_name="logins.json" OR Filesystem.file_name="cookies.sqlite") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where stores>=2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Filesystem.file_name) as stores values(Filesystem.file_name) as files min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*google-chrome*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*chromium*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*BraveSoftware*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*.mozilla*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Microsoft*Edge*") (Filesystem.file_name="Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="Cookies" OR Filesystem.file_name="Web Data" OR Filesystem.file_name="key4.db" OR Filesystem.file_name="logins.json" OR Filesystem.file_name="cookies.sqlite") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where stores>=2 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
ChocoPoC discovery: bulk enumeration of docs/DB files and shell history by a Python process AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ChocoPoC collection stage — a Python process reading a large number of text/markdown/database files and shell-history files in a short window, matching the RAT's file-search and shell-history capabilities. Distinguished from benign PoC execution by the volume and file-type mix. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit collection list (text files, markdown docs, database files, shell history) as the file-type filter, and a python-initiated >=20-distinct-file burst in 5m to separate targeted harvesting from a PoC that legitimately reads a couple of docs. Sigma skipped: this is a count/threshold + time-window detection, not single-event-shape. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chocopoc-malware-delivered-via-trojanized-poc-exploits/
ATT&CKT1083 T1005 T1552.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data-science/ETL python jobs that legitimately read many .csv/.db/.sqlite files
  • Documentation build tools (mkdocs/sphinx) walking a repo full of .md files
  • A developer's local test suite that opens many fixture .json/.sqlite files
  • Backup or indexing utilities implemented in python scanning the home directory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("mkdocs","sphinx-build","pytest","jupyter","dvc","airflow"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the SampleCmd and the parent chain — a python process from a freshly-cloned PoC repo reading home-directory .bash_history and scattered .db/.md files is malicious versus a project-scoped build tool. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the process, and preserve the enumerated file list for scoping data exposure (docs, DBs, and shell history often contain secrets). 3) Hunt: correlate to the skytext install (UC1/UC2), Mapbox exfil (UC3), and browser-secret theft (UC4) on the same host/user, then rotate any credentials found in the accessed shell-history/config files.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3")
| where (FileName endswith ".md" or FileName endswith ".txt" or FileName endswith ".db" or FileName endswith ".sqlite" or FileName endswith ".sqlite3" or FileName in~ (".bash_history",".zsh_history",".python_history"))
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize DistinctFiles = dcount(FolderPath), Exts = make_set(tostring(extract(@"(\.[^.\\/]+)$", 1, FileName)), 10), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctFiles >= 20
| order by bin_Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python","python3")
| where (TargetFileName endswith ".md" or TargetFileName endswith ".txt" or TargetFileName endswith ".db" or TargetFileName endswith ".sqlite" or TargetFileName endswith ".sqlite3" or TargetFileName in~ (".bash_history",".zsh_history",".python_history"))
| summarize DistinctFiles = dcount(TargetFilePath), SampleCmd = any(ActingProcessCommandLine) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessId, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctFiles >= 20
| order by bin_TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(find OR grep OR rg OR ls) @process.command_line:(*.md* OR *.sqlite* OR *.db* OR *.bash_history* OR *.zsh_history*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo | ContextImageFileName=/python/i | TargetFileName=/(\.(md|txt|db|sqlite3?)$|\.(bash|zsh|python)_history$)/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true)) | _count >= 20
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinctFiles values(Filesystem.file_name) as files from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.md" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.db" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.sqlite" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.sqlite3" OR Filesystem.file_name=".bash_history" OR Filesystem.file_name=".zsh_history" OR Filesystem.file_name=".python_history") by _time span=5m Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where distinctFiles>=20
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Filesystem.file_path) as distinctFiles values(Filesystem.file_name) as files from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.md" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.txt" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.db" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.sqlite" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.sqlite3" OR Filesystem.file_name=".bash_history" OR Filesystem.file_name=".zsh_history" OR Filesystem.file_name=".python_history") by _time span=5m Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where distinctFiles>=20
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent

| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

logsource:

Unpatched Argo CD Repo-Server Flaw Could Let Attackers Take Over Kubernetes Clusters

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 13 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Argo CD, a widely used tool for deploying software to Kubernetes, has an unpatched flaw in its repo-server component that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code, provided they can reach the component's internal network port. Synacktiv, which found the bug, says it can lead to a full cluster takeover. There is no fix and no CVE. The firm says it reported the flaw to Argo CD's maintainers in

kustomize invoked with --helm-command pointing to a non-helm executable (Argo CD repo-server RCE primitive) AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact exploitation primitive Synacktiv described against Argo CD repo-server: an unauthenticated GenerateManifest request sets kustomize's --helm-command flag to an attacker-supplied script instead of the helm binary, so kustomize executes arbitrary code. Fires when kustomize runs with --helm-command whose value is not the helm binary. Rationale: Anchored on the two article-specific strings 'kustomize' and '--helm-command'; the negative match on a value ending in 'helm' isolates the attacker's script substitution from Argo CD's own legitimate helm inflation. Cross-checked against the Synacktiv/THN write-up and Argo CD kustomize docs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/kustomize/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Config Management Plugin that wraps helm via a custom path still named helm (excluded by the helm-value filter)
  • A cluster genuinely relocating the helm binary to a wrapper script named e.g. helm-wrapper.sh for private-registry auth
  • Kustomize build tests in CI running inside the same telemetry scope
  • Air-gapped installs pointing --helm-command at a vendored helm under a nonstandard path (validate the value is really helm)
Suppression filter
| where not(ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)--helm-command[ =]+\S*/?helm(file)?\b")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and resolve what the --helm-command value points to; if it is a shell script, a /tmp or /dev/shm path, or a fetched artifact, treat as active exploitation. Capture the repo-server pod/node name. 2) Contain: cordon the node, kill the repo-server pod, and immediately apply the Argo CD network policies (networkPolicy.create=true) so only Argo CD components can reach repo-server and Redis. Rotate the Redis password and any Git repo credentials the repo-server held. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same pod for outbound egress, Redis (6379) connections, and secret reads in the argocd namespace; review recent Application syncs for attacker-supplied workloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "kustomize" or ProcessCommandLine has "kustomize"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command"
| where not(ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)--helm-command[ =]+\S*/?helm\b")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has "kustomize" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "kustomize"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command"
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)--helm-command[ =]+\S*/?helm\b")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Argo CD Repo-Server Exploitation Attempt AIExploitation Medium
Detects the argocd-repo-server (or the kustomize/helm processes it spawns) launching shells or download/recon tooling outside the normal git+helm+kustomize manifest-generation workflow. This is the post-exploitation shape of the unauthenticated repo-server RCE — a script pulled from an attacker Git repo executing on repo-server. Rationale: Uses the article's named component (argocd-repo-server) and the tools it legitimately drives (kustomize, helm) as the parent scope, so the child shell/download-tool set is the differentiator between benign manifest generation and post-RCE tooling. Corroborated by Synacktiv/THN disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Config Management Plugins that legitimately shell out (sh -c) to render manifests
  • Init/entrypoint scripts in the repo-server image invoking sh at startup
  • helm pulling charts via an http(s) proxy helper that calls curl
  • Admin exec into the repo-server pod for troubleshooting (kubectl exec spawning bash)
  • Custom tooling images that vendor python for template rendering
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("kubectl exec","/entrypoint","cmp-server")) and not(FileName in~ ("sh") and ProcessCommandLine has "argocd-cmp")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — a curl/wget to an external host, a base64-decoded payload, or an interactive shell from repo-server is high confidence. Correlate against a same-time --helm-command event and outbound egress from the pod. 2) Contain: delete the repo-server pod, enable Argo CD network policies, and rotate Redis + Git credentials. 3) Hunt: check the argocd namespace for anomalous secret reads, Redis cache writes to the 'mfst' key, and newly created/edited Applications pointing at untrusted repos.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","repo-server","kustomize","helm") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "argocd-repo-server"
| where FileName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","chmod","base64")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","repo-server","kustomize","helm")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("bash","sh","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","python","python3","perl","chmod","base64")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Argo CD repo-server pod initiating anomalous outbound egress (attacker script fetch / C2) AICommand & Control Medium
Surfaces the argocd-repo-server pod making outbound connections to non-private, non-Git/-registry destinations — the network shape of a --helm-command script being fetched from an attacker Git repo, or of C2 after repo-server RCE. Baselines against known Git/registry hosts and private RFC1918 ranges. Rationale: Pivots on the named repo-server pod hostname and excludes RFC1918 + the standard Git/registry hosts repo-server legitimately reaches, so remaining public egress is the attacker-repo fetch or C2. Sentinel version keyed on ImNetworkSession.SrcHostname (ImNetworkSession carries no process-name column). Corroborated by Synacktiv/THN. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • repo-server pulling Helm charts or Git repos hosted on a self-managed public host not in the allowlist
  • Public OCI registry (self-hosted Harbor/Artifactory on a public IP) for chart pulls
  • Telemetry/metrics agents co-located in the pod calling home
  • Corporate proxy egress where the proxy IP is public
  • A legitimately configured external Helm repository added after the baseline
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the destination IP/URL and port; a raw IP, a paste/file-host, or a nonstandard port from repo-server is high confidence. Check whether the connection was initiated by a shell/curl child rather than helm/kustomize. 2) Contain: apply Argo CD network policies to isolate repo-server, delete the pod, block the destination at egress, and rotate Redis/Git secrets. 3) Hunt: correlate with --helm-command execution and shell spawns on the same pod, and review Redis 'mfst' cache writes and recent Application syncs.

| where not(RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com","gitlab.com","bitbucket.org","ghcr.io","docker.io","registry-1.docker.io","quay.io"))

| order by FirstSeen desc

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber,20) by SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by FirstSeen desc

Suspicious Git Repository Credential Access from Argo CD AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects a non-Argo-CD principal reading or enumerating multiple Kubernetes Secrets in the argocd namespace (repo credentials, Redis password, service-account tokens) via the API server. This is the credential-theft step Synacktiv used after repo-server RCE and the abuse surface of CVE-2025-55190 / CVE-2026-42880. Rationale: Grounded in the article's post-exploit step (reading the Redis password from the argocd namespace) and the two follow-on CVEs about secret/credential exposure; scopes to the argocd namespace and excludes Argo CD's own service accounts so remaining bulk secret reads are anomalous. Corroborated by THN and the Cycode CVE-2024-31989 write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://cycode.com/blog/revealing-argo-cd-critical-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1552.007 T1555
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A cluster admin (human UPN) legitimately auditing argocd secrets during troubleshooting
  • A backup/DR tool (Velero) with cluster-wide secret read enumerating argocd secrets
  • A policy/compliance scanner (Kyverno, Trivy-operator) listing secrets
  • GitOps migration tooling reading repo-credential secrets
  • External-secrets operator reconciling secrets in the argocd namespace
Suppression filter
| where Username !endswith "velero" and UserAgent !has_any ("velero","kyverno","trivy","external-secrets") and Username !contains "@"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the principal (Username/UserAgent) and whether it maps to a known admin, backup, or scanner. A service-account token from an unrelated namespace or a raw kubectl UA enumerating repo-creds/redis secrets is high confidence. 2) Contain: revoke/rotate the affected secrets (Git repo creds, Redis password), invalidate the offending token, and apply network policies to isolate Redis/repo-server. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same principal for RoleBinding changes, Application/ApplicationSet edits, and Redis cache writes; check repo-server for RCE indicators.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| where Verb in ("get","list","watch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "secrets"
| where tostring(ObjectRef.namespace) == "argocd"
| where Username !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:"
| where Username !in ("system:apiserver")
| summarize SecretCount=dcount(tostring(ObjectRef.name)), Secrets=make_set(tostring(ObjectRef.name),50), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), UserAgents=make_set(UserAgent,10) by Username
| where SecretCount >= 3  // 3 = enumeration of multiple argocd secrets by a non-argocd principal
| order by FirstSeen desc
