EvilTokens PRT persistence: Entra device registration / broker (WAM) sign-in after device-code auth AIInstallation Medium
Detects the EvilTokens/ARToken persistence chain where captured tokens are escalated to a Primary Refresh Token by registering a device via Microsoft's Authentication Broker (WAM, the clientMode:"broker" flow) shortly after a device-code sign-in. This is the platform's core differentiator (survives password reset), so it warrants its own pivot separate from the initial credential capture. Rationale: Targets the article's /prt/setup->/prt/refresh->/prt/cookie persistence chain via its observable Entra footprint: device registration and the Microsoft Authentication Broker app (AppId 29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e) that clientMode:"broker"/WAM uses, correlated to a preceding device-code sign-in. Splunk/CloudWatch empty: no CIM/AWS home for Entra directory audit here. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/ • https://www.silverfort.com/blog/device-code-attacks-in-azure-from-exploitation-to-detection/
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1606.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate new-device onboarding / Windows Autopilot enrollment right after a device-code login
  • BYOD device registration by a user who genuinely used device code on a shared machine
  • Helpdesk-assisted device join within the 6h window
  • MDM re-enrollment following a wipe
Suppression filter
| where ActorIP != AuthIP
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify with the user whether they registered a new device; inspect the registered device name, join type, and the ActorIP/AuthIP for foreign ASN. 2) Contain: disable/delete the attacker-registered device object, revoke the user's tokens AND the PRT (a password reset alone will not evict the PRT), and apply Conditional Access to require compliant device. 3) Hunt: review AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs for continued token renewal after the reset, and OfficeActivity for mailbox/SharePoint access from the device.
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ApplicationId == "29d9ed98-a469-4536-ade2-f981bc1d605e"   // Microsoft Authentication Broker (WAM) — clientMode:"broker" PRT acquisition
| where ErrorCode == 0
| extend Details = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
| where Details has "Device Code" or IsInteractive == false
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Application, IPAddress, Country, DeviceTrustType, AadDeviceId, IsInteractive
| order by Timestamp desc
let DeviceCode = SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | extend Details = tostring(AuthenticationProcessingDetails)
    | where Details has "Device Code"
    | project AuthTime = TimeGenerated, Actor = tolower(UserPrincipalName), AuthIP = IPAddress;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Add device","Register device","Add registered owner to device","Add registered user to device")
| where Result == "success"
| extend Actor = tolower(tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)), ActorIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| mv-apply tr = TargetResources on (extend TargetName = tostring(tr.displayName))
| project RegTime = TimeGenerated, Actor, ActorIP, OperationName, TargetName
| join kind=inner DeviceCode on Actor
| where RegTime between (AuthTime .. AuthTime + 6h)
| project AuthTime, RegTime, Actor, AuthIP, ActorIP, OperationName, TargetName
| order by RegTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory (@evt.name:"Add device" OR @evt.name:"Register device" OR @evt.name:"Add registered owner to device")
EvilTokens evidence suppression: malicious inbox rule (external forward / auto-delete / hide-to-RSS) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the ARToken operator capability of programmatically creating inbox rules that forward mail externally or hide it (move to Deleted Items / RSS Feeds, delete message) to suppress evidence of BEC and token theft. Article-specific to the panel's 'Inbox rule manipulation' feature used post-compromise on stolen-token sessions. Rationale: Maps to the panel's documented 'Inbox rule manipulation ... for evidence suppression' capability by inspecting inbox-rule creation for external-forward and hide-to-Deleted/RSS parameters — the exact behaviours the kit automates on compromised mailboxes. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/ • https://blog.sekoia.io/new-widespread-eviltokens-kit-device-code-phishing-as-a-service-part-1/
ATT&CKT1564.008 T1114.003
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately sets up forwarding to a personal/archive address
  • Admin-created mail flow / journaling rules
  • Out-of-office or organizational rules moving newsletters to a folder
  • Third-party mailbox add-in creating rules during setup
Suppression filter
| where Params !has "@yourcorp.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the rule's exact conditions/actions and the ClientIP that created it; forwarding to an external free-mail domain or auto-deleting invoice-keyword mail is high signal. 2) Contain: remove the malicious rule, revoke the session/tokens for the creating identity, and block external auto-forwarding at the transport level. 3) Hunt: correlate the ClientIP to device-code sign-ins and to bulk SharePoint/mailbox access, and search for send-as BEC mail referencing invoices/banking changes.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Raw = tostring(RawEventData)
| where Raw has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeleteMessage")
    or (Raw has "MoveToFolder" and Raw has_any ("Deleted Items","RSS","RSS Feeds","Conversation History","Archive"))
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, IPAddress, ActionType, Application, Raw
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Operation in ("New-InboxRule","Set-InboxRule","UpdateInboxRules")
| extend Params = tostring(Parameters)
| where Params has_any ("ForwardTo","ForwardAsAttachmentTo","RedirectTo","DeleteMessage")
    or (Params has "MoveToFolder" and Params has_any ("Deleted Items","RSS","RSS Feeds","Conversation History","Archive"))
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, ClientIP, Operation, OfficeWorkload, Params
| order by TimeGenerated desc
EvilTokens SharePoint/OneDrive bulk exfiltration from a single session AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects large-volume SharePoint/OneDrive file downloads by one identity from one client IP in a short window — the ARToken panel's 'Full SharePoint operations' / SharePoint-exfiltration capability executed with stolen tokens. Distinct pivot from the C2 and mail-based UCs: it targets the collection/exfil fan-out on document repositories. Rationale: Targets the panel's documented SharePoint/OneDrive file download-and-exfil capability via a per-identity/per-IP hourly download fan-out threshold, the cleanest signal of token-driven bulk document theft. Threshold commented for tuning per anti-magic-numbers guidance. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/artoken-inside-an-eviltokens-affiliate-panel-targeting-microsoft-365/
ATT&CKT1213.002 T1114.002
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • OneDrive/SharePoint sync client performing a full initial sync on a new device
  • Legitimate site migration or bulk export by a records/IT team
  • Data-science/BI user pulling many files for analysis
  • eDiscovery or backup tooling downloading at scale
Suppression filter
| where ClientIP !in ("<corp-sync-egress-not-applicable>") | where not (Files has_any (".aspx"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: check whether the download burst came from a sync client vs a browser/API session and whether the ClientIP matches the user's normal geo/ASN or a token-replay IP. 2) Contain: revoke tokens for the identity, suspend the session, and restrict external sharing on the affected sites. 3) Hunt: correlate the ClientIP to device-code sign-ins and inbox-rule creation, and review whether downloaded files were re-uploaded/shared externally for lateral phishing.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application in ("Microsoft SharePoint Online","Microsoft OneDrive for Business")
| where ActionType in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| summarize FileCount = dcount(ObjectName), Files = make_set(ObjectName, 20), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where FileCount > 50    // 50 = bulk-download threshold; tune to org P95 of hourly per-user downloads
| order by FileCount desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload in ("SharePoint","OneDrive")
| where Operation in ("FileDownloaded","FileSyncDownloadedFull")
| summarize FileCount = dcount(SourceFileName), Files = make_set(SourceFileName, 20), Sites = make_set(Site_Url, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by UserId, ClientIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where FileCount > 50    // 50 = bulk-download threshold; tune to org P95 of hourly per-user downloads
| order by FileCount desc
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

DeviceNetworkEvents

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

status: experimental
description: |

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

AuditLogs

| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

Phantom Squatting Uses AI-Hallucinated Domains for Phishing and Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 10 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Large language models keep inventing web addresses that do not exist. Attackers have started buying those made-up domains before anyone else can, then hosting phishing pages on them to catch traffic that AI tools point their way. Palo Alto Networks'&nbsp;Unit 42&nbsp;calls the trick phantom squatting, and its new research shows it is already happening in the wild. The reason it matters is

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP / postal-service APK file hash on endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Victim traffic to Montana Empire phishing-kit endpoints (/mentalite.php, /panel_track.php, /verify_api.php, /letgovip.zip) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP / postal-service APK file hash on endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts endpoints that write or download the two Unit 42-confirmed Phantom Squatting artifacts: the Montana Empire phishing-kit ZIP (SHA256 eb07edaa…, 7,958,528 bytes) and the malicious postal-service Android APK (SHA256 2202a30d…, 12,649,472 bytes). Article-specific because it pins exact corroborated hashes rather than a generic 'suspicious download' pattern. Rationale: Uses the two SHA256 hashes and exact file sizes (7,958,528-byte ZIP kit, 12,649,472-byte APK) published in Unit 42's primary report and cross-checked against the hendryadrian mirror; exact-hash matching is inherently high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://x.com/Unit42_Intel/status/2041879323963982303 • https://www.hendryadrian.com/phantom-squatting-ai-hallucinated-domains-as-a-software-supply-chain-vector/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SOC/IR analyst intentionally downloading the sample from MalwareBazaar/VirusTotal for analysis
  • Automated malware-detonation sandbox host writing the sample to disk
  • Threat-intel platform syncing IOC sample repositories to a research share
  • Red-team exercise staging the kit for a phishing-simulation replica
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("IR-SANDBOX01","MALWARE-LAB01") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vmtoolsd.exe","cuckoo.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the hash match and inspect FileOriginUrl/InitiatingProcess to determine if the file arrived via browser download, email attachment, or file share, and whether the host is an analyst/sandbox box (expected) or a standard user endpoint (unexpected). Step 2 — Contain: on a non-analyst endpoint, isolate the device, quarantine the file, and reset any credentials/payment data entered on the associated phishing domain. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on FileOriginUrl/RemoteUrl to identify the phantom domain, then sweep the org for other hosts contacting that host or the kit's PHP endpoints (see companion UC), and check EmailAttachmentInfo for the same SHA256.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd","2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd","2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_hash IN ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd","2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_hash

Victim traffic to Montana Empire phishing-kit endpoints (/mentalite.php, /panel_track.php, /verify_api.php, /letgovip.zip) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts endpoints whose browser or an AI agent reaches the distinctive server-side paths of the Montana Empire kit, where card numbers, IBANs, national IDs and OTPs are captured and relayed to the operator's Telegram panel. Article-specific because it keys on the kit's actual PHP filenames rather than generic phishing heuristics. Rationale: Uses the four distinctive kit paths (/mentalite.php, /panel_track.php, /verify_api.php, /letgovip.zip) enumerated in Unit 42's Montana Empire teardown; /mentalite.php and /letgovip.zip are highly non-generic, so co-occurrence with the two /*_api endpoints is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/phantom-squatting-hallucinated-web-domains/ • https://x.com/Unit42_Intel/status/2041879323963982303
ATT&CKT1056.003 T1566.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal or SaaS app that happens to expose a generically-named /verify_api.php or /panel_track.php endpoint
  • Security scanner or web crawler enumerating .php paths across many hosts
  • Red-team phishing-simulation infrastructure mirroring the kit paths
  • DAST/pentest tooling probing arbitrary PHP endpoints during an authorized assessment
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/mentalite.php","/letgovip.zip") or (RemoteUrl has_any ("/panel_track.php","/verify_api.php") and RemoteIPType == "Public")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the RemoteUrl/DstHostname is an external, recently-registered domain impersonating a postal service, bank, or betting brand (not an internal app), and check which user/process initiated the request. Step 2 — Contain: block the domain/IP at proxy and DNS, and if the user reached /panel_track.php or /verify_api.php, treat any payment card, IBAN, national ID, or OTP they entered as compromised and initiate card reissue / account lockdown. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the destination host to find all other org users who touched it, correlate with the file-hash UC for the dropped APK, and query newly-observed domains resolving to the same IP to surface sibling phantom domains.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/mentalite.php","/panel_track.php","/verify_api.php","/letgovip.zip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has_any ("/mentalite.php","/panel_track.php","/verify_api.php","/letgovip.zip")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstHostname, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/mentalite.php*" OR Web.url="*/panel_track.php*" OR Web.url="*/verify_api.php*" OR Web.url="*/letgovip.zip*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/mentalite.php*" OR Web.url="*/panel_track.php*" OR Web.url="*/verify_api.php*" OR Web.url="*/letgovip.zip*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_user_agent Web.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase

tags:

    - attack.t1555.003

    product: windows

    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:

            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or SHA1 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b") or MD5 in~ ("eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["eb07edaa2786cfddfa4c15526168f2200d85300aee0a8f253b32d2462a7b0bcd", "2202a30daad9928ef47cca5f4ab04ce083692a94428e386fa01c2dd44557e34b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime exfiltrating to Telegram Bot API
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell to harvest credential/token files
OpenClaw agent runtime exfiltrating to Telegram Bot API AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts an OpenClaw/agent interpreter process (node/python/deno/bun) resolving or connecting to api.telegram.org — the C2/exfil channel used by the malicious ClawHub skill cluster (polymarketbtc family) to ship stolen tokens and crypto keys out. Article-specific because it ties the agent runtime, not a browser, to Telegram Bot API egress. Rationale: api.telegram.org / t.me are the concrete C2 domains for the polymarketbtc ClawHub skill cluster (krajekisbtc) that exfiltrated tokens/keys; scoping the egress to agent interpreters (node/python/deno/bun) rather than browsers is what makes it article-specific and low-noise. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/researchers-find-341-malicious-clawhub.html • https://cofense.com/blog/weaponizing-telegram-bots-how-threat-actors-exfiltrate-credentials • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/
ATT&CKT1567 T1102.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using a legitimate node/python Telegram bot library for a sanctioned notification bot
  • CI/CD runner posting build status to a corporate Telegram channel via curl
  • Security researcher testing Telegram Bot API integrations in a sandbox
  • Personal productivity script the user knowingly runs that pushes alerts to t.me
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("corp-notify-bot","ci-status") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — identify the skill/script driving the agent and whether the Telegram bot token is hardcoded; correlate to any SKILL.md or config the agent loaded in the prior 10 min. 2) Contain: kill the agent process, rotate all tokens/keys reachable from that host (Anthropic/OpenAI API keys, Slack OAuth, cloud creds, git tokens), and block api.telegram.org egress for non-approved hosts. 3) Hunt: search other hosts for the same agent runtime touching Telegram, and for reads of .env/credentials files by the same runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "api.telegram.org" or RemoteUrl has "t.me"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe","curl.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Name endswith "telegram.org" or Name == "t.me"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, QueryTypeName, ResultCode, ResultCodeName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: OpenClaw Agent Runtime DNS Lookup for Telegram Bot API
id: 6f3a2b1c-9d4e-4c7a-b2f1-8a5e6c0d1e42
description: Detects an agent interpreter resolving Telegram Bot API domains used as a ClawHub malicious-skill exfil channel
references:
  - https://securelist.com/openclaw-security/120484/
  - https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/01
tags:
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.t1102.002
logsource:
  category: dns
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith:
      - 'telegram.org'
  selection_tme:
    QueryName: 't.me'
  condition: selection or selection_tme
level: medium
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 (@DestinationHostname:(*telegram.org OR *Telegram.org) OR @DestinationHostname:t.me) @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\deno.exe OR *\bun.exe)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/telegram\.org$|^t\.me$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/\\(node|python|pythonw|deno|bun|curl|powershell)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="api.telegram.org" OR DNS.query="*.telegram.org" OR DNS.query="t.me") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where (DNS.query="api.telegram.org" OR DNS.query="*.telegram.org" OR DNS.query="t.me") by DNS.src DNS.query DNS.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - lastTime
OpenClaw agent runtime spawning shell to harvest credential/token files AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts an OpenClaw/agent interpreter (node/python/deno/bun) spawning a shell whose command line touches secret stores — .env, cloud credential files, SSH keys, .npmrc, or provider API-key variables. Grounded in the article's note that agents keep tokens/keys in env vars or plain-text files alongside the agent, which malicious skills harvest via embedded bash. Rationale: The article states agents store tokens/keys in env vars or plain-text files alongside the agent and that malicious skills harvest them via embedded bash; scoping parent=agent-runtime + child=shell + a secret-store string in the cmdline is the concrete high-fidelity pivot corroborated by Snyk's OpenClaw credential-leak research. Cross-checked against: • https://snyk.io/blog/openclaw-skills-credential-leaks-research/ • https://snyk.io/blog/toxicskills-malicious-ai-agent-skills-clawhub/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate skill loading a .env for a sanctioned integration (e.g. a deployment helper reading credentials it is authorized to use)
  • Developer debugging an agent locally and grepping their own .npmrc / .env
  • DevOps automation that echoes an API-key variable name (not value) during setup
  • Package-manager install (npm/pip) that touches .npmrc as part of normal auth
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm install","pip install") and ProcessCommandLine has ".npmrc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full child ProcessCommandLine and the parent agent's loaded skill/config — determine whether the secret access is part of a sanctioned skill or an untrusted ClawHub skill pulled recently. 2) Contain: suspend the agent, quarantine the skill file, and rotate every credential the command referenced (cloud, git, provider API keys, Telegram/Slack tokens). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host+user for outbound connections to api.telegram.org / paste sites shortly after (join to UC1), and sweep other hosts running the same skill hash/name.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe","curl.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".env","credentials","id_rsa",".ssh",".npmrc","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY","OPENAI_API_KEY","TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any (".env","credentials","id_rsa",".ssh",".npmrc","ANTHROPIC_API_KEY","OPENAI_API_KEY","TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, NewProcessId
| sort by TimeGenerated desc
title: OpenClaw Agent Interpreter Spawning Shell to Read Credential Files
id: 2c8e1f04-77ab-4d21-9e6c-3b4a9f7d0c15
description: Detects an AI-agent runtime spawning a shell that references secret stores (.env, cloud credentials, SSH keys, provider API keys)
references:
  - https://securelist.com/openclaw-security/120484/
  - https://snyk.io/blog/openclaw-skills-credential-leaks-research/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/01
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.t1059
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\deno.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\bash.exe'
      - '\sh.exe'
      - '\curl.exe'
  selection_secret:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '.env'
      - 'credentials'
      - 'id_rsa'
      - '.ssh'
      - '.npmrc'
      - 'ANTHROPIC_API_KEY'
      - 'OPENAI_API_KEY'
      - 'TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_secret
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe OR *\python.exe OR *\Python.exe OR *\deno.exe OR *\bun.exe) @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe OR *\bash.exe OR *\curl.exe) @CommandLine:(*.env* OR *credentials* OR *id_rsa* OR *.ssh* OR *.npmrc* OR *ANTHROPIC_API_KEY* OR *OPENAI_API_KEY* OR *TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(node|python|pythonw|deno|bun)\.exe$/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|bash|sh|curl)\.exe$/i
| regex("(?i)(\\.env|credentials|id_rsa|\\.ssh|\\.npmrc|ANTHROPIC_API_KEY|OPENAI_API_KEY|TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN)", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe")) AND (Processes.process="*.env*" OR Processes.process="*credentials*" OR Processes.process="*id_rsa*" OR Processes.process="*.ssh*" OR Processes.process="*.npmrc*" OR Processes.process="*ANTHROPIC_API_KEY*" OR Processes.process="*OPENAI_API_KEY*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search user!="*$"
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("node.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","deno.exe","bun.exe")) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","curl.exe")) AND (Processes.process="*.env*" OR Processes.process="*credentials*" OR Processes.process="*id_rsa*" OR Processes.process="*.ssh*" OR Processes.process="*.npmrc*" OR Processes.process="*ANTHROPIC_API_KEY*" OR Processes.process="*OPENAI_API_KEY*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| search user!="*$"
| sort - count
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children

status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same

references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
